findings.title: Calendar update uses actor credentials instead of booking owner credentials
findings.body: The handler fetches booking.user with destinationCalendar and credentials, but then builds EventManager from ctx.user and calls getUsersCredentials(ctx.user). For any actor other than the organizer—especially the team-admin and attendee cases allowed by the permission check—this tries to update the organizer's calendar event using the actor's calendar credentials. If the actor has no matching calendar credentials, the mutation can fail after attendees have already been written; otherwise the organizer's calendar event is not updated correctly. Use the booking owner/organizer credentials for this booking.

findings.title: Team admin/owner check requires both admin and owner
findings.body: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`, so a team admin who is not also an owner is denied access. Depending on the helper semantics, an owner who is not also an admin may also be denied. This makes the new endpoint return FORBIDDEN for legitimate team admins. This should be an OR check, and the team permission check should only be used when the booking has a team event type.

findings.title: Guest filtering is case-sensitive and does not dedupe submitted emails
findings.body: `uniqueGuests` only excludes exact-case matches against existing attendee emails, and compares non-normalized guest emails against a lower-cased BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS list. An attacker can bypass the blacklist by changing case and can create duplicate attendees whose emails differ only by case. The filter also only checks against the pre-update attendee list, so duplicate emails inside the submitted `guests` array all pass and are inserted. Emails should be normalized to lower case and deduped both within the input and against existing attendees server-side.

findings.title: Emails use raw guests list instead of filtered uniqueGuests
findings.body: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the original client input, while only `uniqueGuests` were inserted. If a caller includes an existing attendee's email, that attendee is still present in `newGuests`, so sendAddGuestsEmails classifies them as a newly added guest and sends them AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of the guest-added notification. It also bypasses the filtering done above. Pass `uniqueGuests` to the email function.

findings.title: New guest email path ignores disabled standard email settings
findings.body: Unlike sendScheduledEmails and sendLocationChangeEmails, sendAddGuestsEmails has no eventTypeMetadata parameter and unconditionally sends OrganizerAddGuestsEmail and attendee emails. Users who configured eventType.metadata.disableStandardEmails for host or attendee emails will still receive these guest-added emails, breaking the existing opt-out contract. Accept metadata and guard host/attendee sends with eventTypeDisableHostEmail and eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail.

findings.title: No limit on guest count or invite rate
findings.body: The only validation is that each array item looks like an email; there is no maximum guest count or per-booking/rate limit. Any authorized attendee or organizer can submit an arbitrarily large list, causing a large createMany, calendar fan-out, and mass emails to arbitrary addresses from Cal.com. Add a reasonable max and enforce rate limiting on this mutation.

findings.title: Error toast can show 'undefined:' instead of fallback message
findings.body: `const message = `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`` always produces a non-empty string, so the `|| t('unable_to_add_guests')` fallback is unreachable. When err.data is absent, users see `undefined: <message>` rather than the intended fallback. Build the message conditionally and use the fallback when no usable error text exists.
